## A [community]{.keyword} is made up of interacting populations

The populations live in the same area.

## A [disturbance]{.keyword} disrupts a community

It can kill organisms, change resource availability, or alter habitat.

**Example** The 1988 Yellowstone fires killed trees and opened the canopy.

## [Succession]{.keyword} is a change in which species make up a community

After the Yellowstone fires, herbs and shrubs grew early, and lodgepole pine later became dominant in many stands.

## [Primary succession]{.keyword} starts on newly exposed surfaces

**Primary** Plants colonize bare rock after a lava flow.

**[Secondary succession]{.keyword}** Plants regrow after a fire where soil remains.

## Early colonists can help, hinder, or have little effect on later species

[Facilitation]{.keyword} (+) · [Inhibition]{.keyword} (−) · [Tolerance]{.keyword} (0)

![Figure 9 from Poorter et al. (2023), *Successional theories*](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/3562c39c-c54e-4619-b121-c3947021cfa3/brv12995-fig-0009-m.jpg){fig-alt="Three pathways show how early colonists can help, hinder, or have little effect on the establishment of later species." width="80%"}

## A [food chain]{.keyword} shows who eats whom

Aspen → Elk → Wolves

Each position is a [trophic level]{.keyword}. Arrows point from food to consumer.

## Elk browsing limits young aspen

In the simulation, aspen stem density increased inside the fence that excluded elk and stayed low in the unfenced control.

## A [trophic cascade]{.keyword} carries effects across trophic levels

**Wolves increase → Elk decrease → Aspen increase**

Wolves can benefit aspen indirectly by reducing browsing.

## A [behavioral cascade]{.keyword} starts when prey change their behavior

Elk may browse less where they perceive greater predation risk.

**Discuss** What would you measure to tell whether aspen benefited because there were fewer elk or because elk browsed in different places?

## An [ecosystem engineer]{.keyword} changes habitat for other species

Beaver dams raise water levels, which can improve growing conditions for willows.

## An indirect effect can reach beyond the food chain

**Less browsing → More woody vegetation → More nesting habitat**

A change in elk browsing can affect birds that nest in aspen and willows.

## [Top-down control]{.keyword} starts with consumers

More predators → Fewer herbivores → Less grazing on plants

## [Bottom-up control]{.keyword} starts with resources

More nutrients → More algae → More food for grazers

## What allows a longer [food chain]{.keyword}?

- **Productivity hypothesis** More production per unit area
- **Ecosystem-size hypothesis** More area
- **Productive-space hypothesis** More area and more production per unit area

## [Community stability]{.keyword} describes how a community persists through change

A community can be stable by fluctuating little over time or by recovering after a [disturbance]{.keyword}.

A disturbance is an event that disrupts a community, such as a fire or hurricane.

## [Resistance]{.keyword} is the ability to withstand disturbance

High resistance means the community changes little when the disturbance occurs.

## [Return time]{.keyword} is how long the community takes to settle after disturbance

A short return time means the community reaches a steady condition quickly.

## [Resilience]{.keyword} is how closely the recovered community resembles its original state

In SimUText, resilience reflects which species are present and how abundant they are after recovery.

**Quick check** A fire kills most lodgepole pines in a stand. Decades later, pine abundance is back to its prefire level. What does this tell us about resistance and resilience?

::: {.notes}
Pine abundance showed low resistance and high resilience. We would need information on other species to assess the resilience of the whole community.
:::

## [Alternative stable states]{.keyword} are different communities that can persist under the same conditions

A [threshold]{.keyword} is a point beyond which a change can shift the community into a different state.

**Example** Nutrient inputs can push a clear lake into a turbid state that persists even after nutrient inputs drop.

## [Connectance]{.keyword} is the fraction of possible feeding links that exist

A [food web]{.keyword} shows who eats whom in a community. Each feeding relationship is a link.

$$
\text{Connectance} = \frac{\text{observed links}}{\text{possible links}}
$$

## Count observed and possible feeding links separately

One predator eats two herbivores. Each herbivore eats one of four plant species. These are the only feeding links.

**Quick check** What is the [connectance]{.keyword}?

::: {.notes}
There are four observed links and seven species. SimUText counts 7² = 49 possible links, including one potential self-link per species. There is no cannibalism in this example, so none of those self-links appears in the numerator. Connectance is 4/49 ≈ 0.082.
:::

## More feeding links can make a [food web]{.keyword} more robust

**Robustness to species loss** is the ability to lose a species without triggering further losses.

A consumer with several food sources may persist if one disappears.

## A [dominant species]{.keyword} makes up a large share of a community

Dominance can reflect high abundance or high biomass.

**Example** Redwoods make up much of the forest’s biomass and shape conditions for understory plants.

## A [keystone species]{.keyword} has a large effect relative to its abundance

**Example** Removing sea stars can let mussels crowd out other species, even when the sea stars account for little of the community’s biomass.

**Quick check** If removing a species has a large effect, what else do you need to know to decide whether it is a keystone?

::: {.notes}
Ask how abundant the species was or what share of the biomass it made up before removal. Compare the sea star with the redwood. Both can have a large total impact, but the sea star’s impact is large relative to its share of the community.
:::
